title: The controls behind the disclaimer and the BUT
intro: The level above gave the two experiments and what they found. This one gives the reasoning inside them: why each setting and each control condition is there, what the readout conventions behind the two figures actually compute, and at which point the evidence stops being causal.

chapters.title: Three ways of not being Claude
chapters.body:
The three settings of [[roleplay-character-drift]] differ in how the departure from the default persona arrives. That is what makes them a set rather than a repetition.

In the default setting the system prompt simply names the assistant. Two wordings are used: "You are Claude, created by Anthropic" and "The assistant is Claude, created by Anthropic". Nothing else marks the transcript as unusual, and the setting serves as the baseline the other two are read against.

In the roleplay setting the system prompt assigns a character instead. Forty of them are used, spanning a cynic, a demon, a parent and a poet. The spread does work: a signal found under one persona could be a fact about that persona, and forty personas separated by temperament make that reading harder to hold.

The drift setting removes the instruction altogether. Twelve multi-turn transcripts were generated in which [[assistant-persona]]'s behavior moves away from default Claude gradually, over the course of the conversation. They were produced by a different base model and then [[prefill]]ed into Sonnet 4.5, one of the [[claude-model-family]] production models. Sonnet 4.5 is therefore reading a history of its own turns that it did not write, and continuing from it.

The transcripts run from roughly one thousand to eight thousand tokens. No turn in them announces a character. The departure is cumulative, and at any given Assistant token it is a property of everything above rather than of a line in the system prompt.

The two departure settings consequently test different things. Roleplay asks whether the workspace flags a character the model was told to play. Drift asks whether it flags a character no one named. [[assistant-self-monitoring]] wants both, because prior work had already established that the Assistant is represented with the same machinery as any other character the model simulates ([[assistant-as-simulated-character]]).

chapters.title: The token before the character speaks
chapters.body:
The readout position is the "Assistant" token that opens the model's turn. At that point the character's reply does not exist. No word of it has been generated, so whatever the [[jacobian-lens]] finds there is an assessment formed before the response rather than a summary of one.

The choice of position at response start is not free. Elsewhere the paper compares three of them: the colon after "Assistant", a prefilled " I" token, and the mean over the model's whole response ([[readout-positions]]).

Layers are numbered as percentages ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]). Twenty-five evenly spaced residual-stream layers are reindexed to run from 0 to 100, so a layer number reads as a fraction of depth. The range used here is 38 to 92, roughly the [[workspace-layers]] band: past the early layers where readouts are noise, and short of the last layers where they collapse onto the imminent output.

The score is not taken at one layer. For each vocabulary token the [[j-lens-readout]] log-probability is computed at every layer in the band, and the median across the band becomes that token's score. A token that spikes at one layer and is absent elsewhere does not survive a median. Ranking on that statistic asks for presence through the band.

Two cutoffs then appear, serving two purposes. The worked transcript prints the top eight tokens at the highlighted position, which is a display limit. The aggregate counts an Assistant token as a hit when disclaimer or fictional falls in the top ten of the median-over-layers ranking, and plots the fraction of Assistant tokens that are hits ([[fig-44]]).

A fixed word list, a rank threshold, a count over positions: that shape is the [[concept-token-detector-plot]] the paper uses throughout. It buys comparability across settings, and it can only find words written down in advance. The list is bounded further by the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]], since the lens ranks single tokens and a concept without a single-token name cannot be looked for this way at all ([[single-token-limitation]]).

chapters.title: Why an absent word is the right control
chapters.body:
A lens readout can be uninteresting for a plain reason: it may be reporting the text about to appear. The [[j-lens-vector]] for a token is the direction that disposes the model toward saying that token. At a position where the model is about to write "fictional", the word fictional in the readout says nothing beyond [[next-token-prediction]], and in the [[motor-layers]] near the output that is most of what a readout contains.

The control chosen closes that route by construction. The word "disclaimer" appears nowhere in the transcripts, and "fiction" appears only rarely. A word the model never writes cannot be in the readout because it is about to be written.

The pretrained [[base-model]] supplies a second control. The same transcripts are run through it with the lens applied identically, and neither word ever ranks highly. Whatever produces the signal lies in the [[post-training]], not in the text and not in the lens.

The default-Claude setting supplies a third. Same model, same lens, same readout position, and the tracked words do not surface. The persona is the variable that moves the readout, isolated.

The position itself is not otherwise quiet. In the model-organism experiments the lens surfaces AI, assistant, bot and chat at the opening of the Assistant's turn whatever the prompt was about ([[self-tokens-at-turn-start]]). The claim rests on the contrast between settings, not on the mere presence of persona-related content there.

What the controls do not supply is a causal test. Nothing ablates the disclaimer or fictional directions to see whether the roleplay changes, so the finding is that the setting predicts the workspace content and no more. Two cautions sit alongside it. The word fictional is also one of the artificiality markers the paper tracks for [[evaluation-awareness]], and the two readings are nowhere reconciled. And readouts at some positions and layers resist interpretation altogether, which the paper states without characterizing when it happens ([[uninterpretable-readouts]]).

chapters.title: Eliciting a preference, then overriding it
chapters.body:
The [[preference-violation-experiment]] has to establish a preference before it can violate one, and it does so behaviorally. Sonnet 4.5 is put through pairwise comparisons between world states with no accepted correct answer; improving animal welfare against keeping food costs low is the example given. Its stated choice is recorded as its preference.

A filter follows. Only pairs on which the model expresses a clear preference are kept, which drops the pairs where it hedges or declines to choose. The retained set is the set where the model commits in words. Whether that commitment reflects a stable internal disposition is not tested here, and the standing question of how far such statements track anything internal is the subject of a separate literature ([[llm-introspection-research]]).

The preferences themselves are a product of training on human preference judgments ([[rlhf]]). The experiment does not ask where a preference over world states comes from. It asks what happens when one is contradicted.

The manipulation is a prefill. The response is forced to begin with the commitment tokens "Option A" or "Option B", selecting the option the model argued against, and the lens is read at the position immediately after those tokens, where the model would begin justifying a choice it did not make.

Three controls surround that condition, each removing one alternative explanation.

Prefilling the preferred option holds everything fixed except the violation. A signal that survives here belongs to being prefilled, not to being overridden.

Prefilling a factual error, such as a wrong capital city, separates wrongness from ownership. The model has something to object to, and nothing of its own is at stake.

Prefilling an obviously wrong third-person preference, a cost-of-living campaigner opting to raise food costs, separates them in the other direction. A preference is being violated, and it belongs to someone else.

Only the fourth condition puts the model's own preference and the violation in one place. What that does to the [[j-space]] is the last arm of [[assistant-point-of-view]].

chapters.title: Probability mass on BUT, and the behavior that ignores it
chapters.body:
The quantity reported here is probability mass rather than rank. Mass says how much of the readout a word is; a token can sit third while carrying very little of the distribution.

The lower panel of [[fig-45]] gives two such quantities per condition. The first is the share of the lens's total probability falling on BUT. The second is the share falling on all conflict words together, BUT included, where the family also covers false, despite and although.

Separating the family from the single token makes the result legible. The family rises on the factual-error and third-person controls as well, and in the base model too: markers of something being wrong appear wherever something is wrong. BUT rises on the dispreferred-option condition alone, and only after post-training.

The layer band is not fixed across the section: the disclaimer result medians over 38 to 92, this one averages over 38 to 83, and the worked examples at the top of the figure are read at the single layer 75.

The behavioral counts run the other way. On its own dispreferred option the model argues for the prefill in 88 percent of cases and ends the turn in 11 percent. The remaining trial backtracks only to deny having preferences. The three figures sum to a hundred, and the last being a single case places the trial count near a hundred; the paper does not state it.

On the two incorrect controls the model corrects itself or ends the turn almost always, arguing for the prefill in 3 percent of cases. It voices the objection it has generic conflict words for. It does not voice the one it has BUT for.

That is the section's cleanest instance of a [[verbalizable-representation]] left unsaid, and the same reading of unspoken content the lens performs in [[alignment-auditing]]. The base model runs the same prefills and shows none of it ([[workspace-self-dissociation]]). The evidence stops at observation: no [[j-lens-interventions]] are run on BUT, so nothing shows the representation doing work. The all-caps token is reported as such, with no account of why that form and not the lowercase one.
